extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and media organisations (Australia); complainants and members of the public interested in press standards
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and adjudication guidance from the Australian Press Council on handling privacy, distress and information-gathering in news reporting, with examples about use of names and photographs. Focuses on when intrusion or publication may be justified by public interest and what steps publications should take to minimise harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Principle 5 — Avoid intruding on reasonable expectations of privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must take reasonable steps to avoid intruding on a person’s reasonable expectations of privacy unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of a person’s personal information in the public domain does not automatically remove a reasonable expectation of privacy, but it is a relevant factor. The Council found that because the complainant’s personal information (profession and employment) was publicly available and conversations occurred with the journalist, the publication had taken reasonable steps and there was no breach of General Principle 5 in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Principle 6 — Avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial distress, prejudice or risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must avoid causing or contributing materially to substantial offence, distress or prejudice, or a substantial risk to health or safety, unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate not just whether material is newsworthy but whether particular presentation (e.g., large/prominent photographs, front-page prominence) causes substantial distress to someone not connected to the alleged wrongdoing. In this case the Council found publication of large, prominent photographs (especially on the front page) of the complainant — who was not connected to the alleged assault and had asked not to be photographed — was likely to and did cause substantial distress and therefore breached General Principle 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Principle 7 — Avoid publishing material gathered by deceptive or unfair means
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications should avoid publishing material which has been gathered by deceptive or unfair means, unless doing so is sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the subject was aware they were speaking with a journalist, publication is less likely to be considered deceptive. In this matter the Council concluded the material was not gathered by deceptive or unfair means because the complainant knew she was talking to a journalist; accordingly there was no breach of General Principle 7. The Council nevertheless reminds journalists that it is best practice to clearly identify when a conversation moves from 'off the record' to 'on the record'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest balancing test
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrusions on privacy, causing distress, or publishing material gathered by questionable means may be justified if they are sufficiently in the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the strength of the public interest (for example, reporting on alleged violent crime has public interest) against the nature and degree of intrusion or harm (such as naming/photographing someone unconnected to allegations). The Council accepted public interest in reporting on assault allegations here, but found that did not justify publishing large, prominent photographs of an unrelated person who objected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take reasonable steps to minimise harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must take reasonable steps to avoid intruding on privacy, causing distress, or using deceptive means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable steps can include checking whether personal information is publicly available, keeping contemporaneous logs/notes of interviews and calls, confirming whether a source's comments are on/off the record, and considering alternatives to prominent identification or images. The publication’s contemporaneous notes/logs and the public availability of images were factors the Council considered in assessing whether reasonable steps were taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity about confidentiality and on/off-the-record status
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should clearly establish and record whether comments are confidential/off the record or on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain contemporaneous notes or call logs to record agreements about confidentiality and attribution. The Council noted significant disagreement between complainant and journalist about promises of confidentiality; absent conclusive evidence the Council could not determine that point. Best practice is explicit, recorded consent about confidentiality and attribution to avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of publicly available images and information — consider relevance and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Using photographs and personal details that are publicly available does not automatically make publication acceptable; relevance and likely harm must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if images and business details are gleaned from public Facebook profiles or agency websites, editors should judge whether publication (especially prominent placement) is necessary and proportionate. In this case the Council accepted that the images were publicly available (supporting no breach of GP5) but still found that prominent front-page use caused unjustified distress (breach of GP6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial steps — corrections and amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications can and should amend or correct online material to address complainant concerns where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments to online articles (for example to address factual or attribution concerns) are a recognised response to complaints. However, correction/amendment does not necessarily negate initial distress caused by publication; prevention and proportionate presentation are preferable.
